source: Egyptian Health Council - Obstetric and Gynecology Guidelines

guidelines.title: Non-Clinical Interventions to Reduce Overall Cesarean Sections
phrases: The number of women who deliver by Cesarean section has increased steadily in Egypt over the last three decades, from 4.6% in 1992 to 51.8% in 2014.
Cesarean birth is associated with short- and long-term risks that can extend many years beyond the current delivery.
High rates of cesarean section are associated with substantial health-care costs.
Factors contributing to the rise include changes in population characteristics such as increase in multiple pregnancies and advanced maternal age.
Non-clinical factors include women wanting to determine how and when their child is born, fear of medical litigation, and organizational factors.
This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on non-clinical interventions specifically designed to reduce cesarean sections.
Clinical interventions to reduce cesarean section rates are being prepared in a second guideline.
The guideline uses GRADE-Adolopment methodology adapted from WHO guidelines.
Target audience includes obstetricians, midwives, nurses, general practitioners, maternal health program managers, and public health policymakers.

guidelines.title: Rationalizing Cesarean Section in Egypt through 10-Group Classification System
phrases: The 10-group Robson classification system categorizes all pregnant women into 10 mutually exclusive groups based on obstetric characteristics.
Implementing the Robson classification enables standardized audit and comparison of cesarean section rates across facilities.
Each group should be analyzed for its relative size and cesarean section rate to identify areas for intervention.
Group 1 (nulliparous, singleton, cephalic, term, spontaneous labor) and Group 2 (nulliparous, singleton, cephalic, term, induced/CS before labor) are key contributors.
Group 5 (multiparous with previous CS, singleton, cephalic, term) often has the highest CS rate.
Regular audit using Robson classification should be mandatory in all maternity units in Egypt.
Feedback of Robson classification data to clinicians reduces unnecessary cesarean sections.

guidelines.title: Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy & Pregnancy of Unknown Location
phrases: Ectopic pregnancy should be suspected in any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.
Transvaginal ultrasound is the primary diagnostic tool; an empty uterus with beta-hCG >1500-2000 mIU/ml suggests ectopic pregnancy.
Pregnancy of Unknown Location (PUL) is defined as a positive pregnancy test with no visible intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound.
Serial beta-hCG measurements (48-hour interval) are essential for PUL management: rising >53% suggests viable IUP, falling >50% suggests failed PUL.
Methotrexate (single dose 50mg/m2 IM) is first-line medical management for unruptured ectopic pregnancy with beta-hCG <5000 mIU/ml.
Laparoscopic salpingectomy is preferred for ruptured ectopic or failed medical management; salpingostomy may preserve fertility.
Anti-D immunoglobulin should be given to Rh-negative women after ectopic pregnancy management.

guidelines.title: Prevention and Treatment of Hypertension in Pregnancy
phrases: Low-dose aspirin (75-150mg daily) from 12-16 weeks until 36 weeks is recommended for women at high risk of preeclampsia.
High risk factors for preeclampsia include: previous preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, renal disease, autoimmune disease, multiple pregnancy.
Gestational hypertension: new-onset BP ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks without proteinuria or other systemic features.
Preeclampsia: hypertension with proteinuria (≥300mg/24h or PCR ≥30mg/mmol) or maternal organ dysfunction.
Severe hypertension (≥160/110 mmHg) requires urgent treatment to prevent stroke; first-line IV labetalol or hydralazine.
Magnesium sulfate is indicated for seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia and for treatment of eclampsia.
Delivery is the definitive treatment for preeclampsia; timing depends on gestational age, severity, and maternal/fetal condition.
Postpartum monitoring: hypertension can persist or develop de novo up to 6 weeks postpartum.

guidelines.title: Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS): Diagnosis and Management
phrases: PAS includes placenta accreta (adherent to myometrium), increta (invading myometrium), and percreta (penetrating serosa/adjacent organs).
Major risk factors: previous cesarean section, placenta previa, prior uterine surgery, advanced maternal age, multiparity.
Antenatal diagnosis via transvaginal ultrasound (sensitivity 80-90%); MRI adjunctive for posterior placenta or suspected percreta.
Key ultrasound signs: loss of retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, myometrial thinning <1mm, bridging vessels.
Management requires multidisciplinary team: obstetrics, anesthesia, interventional radiology, urology, ICU, blood bank.
Planned preterm delivery at 34-36 weeks after corticosteroid administration; earlier if bleeding or complications.
Cesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ is standard for confirmed PAS; uterine conservation techniques for select cases.
Prophylactic internal iliac balloon catheter or ureteric stents may reduce blood loss in suspected percreta.

guidelines.title: Diagnosis and Management of Endometriosis
phrases: Endometriosis affects 10% of reproductive-age women; defined as endometrial-like tissue outside the uterine cavity.
Classic triad: dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain; infertility present in 30-50% of cases.
Transvaginal ultrasound and MRI can detect endometriomas and deep infiltrating endometriosis; laparoscopy remains gold standard for diagnosis.
First-line medical therapy: NSAIDs for pain, combined oral contraceptives or progestins for suppression.
GnRH agonists/antagonists with add-back therapy for moderate-severe pain refractory to first-line treatment.
Laparoscopic excision of endometriosis improves pain and fertility; hysterectomy with BSO for definitive treatment in completed families.
Deep infiltrating endometriosis involving bowel/bladder requires multidisciplinary surgical planning.
Assisted reproductive technology (IVF) is effective for endometriosis-associated infertility; surgery before IVF not routinely required.

guidelines.title: Clinical Interventions for Prevention of Primary Cesarean Section
phrases: Active phase of labor starts at 6 cm dilation; arrest diagnosed as no cervical change for ≥4 hours with adequate contractions or ≥6 hours with oxytocin.
Latent phase prolongation alone is not indication for cesarean; extended latent phase may be managed expectantly.
Routine amniotomy for labor augmentation not recommended; selective use with oxytocin may shorten labor.
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring increases cesarean rate without improving neonatal outcomes in low-risk women; intermittent auscultation preferred.
Category II fetal heart rate tracings require evaluation and intrauterine resuscitation; Category III requires immediate delivery.
External cephalic version (ECV) at 36-37 weeks reduces breech presentation and cesarean rate; success rate 50-60%.
Trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) success rate 60-80%; VBAC should be offered to eligible women with prior low-transverse CS.
Operative vaginal delivery (forceps/vacuum) reduces cesarean in second stage; requires skilled operator and appropriate indications.
Twin pregnancy with first twin cephalic: vaginal delivery recommended regardless of second twin presentation.
Maternal request cesarean without medical indication not recommended before 39 weeks; shared decision-making required.

guidelines.title: Primary Postpartum Hemorrhage
phrases: PPH defined as blood loss ≥500ml after vaginal birth or ≥1000ml after cesarean section within 24 hours.
Active management of third stage: oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV within 1 minute of delivery, controlled cord traction, uterine massage.
Uterine atony causes 70-80% of PPH; first-line: uterine massage, oxytocin infusion, second-line: ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol.
Tranexamic acid 1g IV within 3 hours of birth reduces death from bleeding by 30%; repeat dose if bleeding continues after 30 minutes.
Intrauterine balloon tamponade (Bakri, Foley) effective for atonic PPH refractory to uterotonics; success rate 80-90%.
Surgical interventions: B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, internal iliac artery ligation, hysterectomy as last resort.
Massive transfusion protocol activation for anticipated blood loss >1500ml or ongoing hemorrhage; 1:1:1 ratio of RBC:FFP:platelets.
Secondary PPH (24h-6weeks): consider retained products, endometritis, subinvolution; ultrasound-guided evacuation if needed.

guidelines.title: Management of Nausea and Vomiting During Pregnancy
phrases: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) affects 70-80% of pregnancies; hyperemesis gravidarum (severe form) affects 0.3-3%.
Diagnosis of hyperemesis: persistent vomiting, ketonuria, weight loss >5% pre-pregnancy weight, electrolyte imbalance.
First-line: dietary modification (small frequent meals, avoid triggers), ginger 250mg qid, acupressure P6 point.
Pharmacological first-line: doxylamine 10mg + pyridoxine 10mg (Diclectin) up to 4 tablets daily; safe in pregnancy.
Second-line: antihistamines (dimenhydrinate, diphenhydramine), metoclopramide, prochlorperazine.
Third-line: ondansetron 4-8mg q8h; limited data on cardiac defects but generally considered safe after first trimester.
Corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 16mg q8h tapering) for refractory hyperemesis after 10 weeks; avoid before 10 weeks due to cleft palate risk.
IV fluids for dehydration; thiamine 100mg before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

guidelines.title: Normal Labor
phrases: First stage: latent phase (0-6cm) variable duration; active phase (≥6cm) progresses at ≥1cm/hour in nulliparas, ≥1.5cm/hour in multiparas.
Second stage: passive descent (full dilation without urge to push) up to 2 hours nullipara/1 hour multipara; active pushing up to 3 hours nullipara/2 hours multipara.
Partogram: alert line at 1cm/hour from 6cm; action line 4 hours after alert line triggers review and intervention.
Intermittent auscultation every 15-30 minutes in active first stage, every 5 minutes in second stage for low-risk women.
Upright positions and mobility in first stage shorten labor; continuous support (doula) reduces cesarean and improves satisfaction.
Epidural analgesia does not increase cesarean rate; may prolong second stage by 15-30 minutes.
Routine episiotomy not recommended; selective use for fetal distress or instrumental delivery.
Delayed cord clamping ≥1 minute improves iron stores; immediate clamping only if resuscitation needed.
Skin-to-skin contact immediately after birth for ≥1 hour promotes breastfeeding and thermoregulation.
